title: Why Every AI Chip Depends on SK Hynix?
core_paradox: The fastest Nvidia GPU on Earth sits idle most of the time waiting for memory, and a 2013 bet nobody wanted gave SK Hynix the keys to the entire AI boom — along with its biggest risk.

thumbnail.headline: THE REAL AI BOTTLENECK
thumbnail.visual_prompt: Clean flat 2D cel-shaded vector illustration of a glowing stacked silicon memory tower beside an AI processor wafer inside a bright modern semiconductor cleanroom, crisp dark ink outlines

seo.summary_hook:
Every flagship AI accelerator Nvidia ships has a secret bottleneck: the math cores are so fast that they spend most of their time waiting for data to arrive. In 2013, SK Hynix built the first High Bandwidth Memory chip for a graphics card market that barely wanted it. Today, that vertical stack of silicon has triggered a global memory shortage from 2025 onward, and made one South Korean memory maker indispensable to the AI boom.

Using a simple kitchen-and-skyscraper analogy, we break down how HBM stacks thin DRAM dies vertically, why 2.5D silicon interposers and Through-Silicon Vias beat flat circuit boards, how capacity limits force massive AI models across multiple GPUs, and why SK Hynix's biggest triumph is also its sharpest vulnerability.
learning_bullets: Why compute got thousands of times faster while memory bandwidth lagged behind.
How SK Hynix and AMD shipped the first High Bandwidth Memory in 2013 and 2015.
How vertical DRAM towers, TSVs, and 2.5D silicon interposers move hundreds of gigabytes per second.
Why limited HBM capacity forces hyperscalers to split models across multi-GPU clusters.
The Tradeoff: why custom pre-sold HBM towers lock memory makers into extreme cyclical risk.

long_scenes.narration: In 2013, engineers at SK Hynix built a strange new memory chip by stacking silicon vertically like a tiny skyscraper. Almost nobody in the PC industry wanted to pay for it. Two years later it shipped inside one niche AMD graphics card. Today, Nvidia cannot ship a flagship AI server without it.
long_scenes.headline: 2013: The Stack Nobody Ordered
long_scenes.subheadline: From one niche AMD GPU in 2015 to the choke point of global AI
long_scenes.ai_image_prompt: Warm flat cel-shaded 2D vector illustration of an engineer desk in Seoul in 2013 with a glowing golden stacked silicon microchip on warm wood, crisp dark ink outlines, sunny window
long_scenes.citation_fact: SK Hynix produced the first HBM chip in 2013; AMD Fiji shipped first in 2015

long_scenes.narration: Starting in 2025, an unprecedented wave of AI data center buildouts triggered a global memory supply shortage. Hyperscalers were not running out of math cores. They were running out of High Bandwidth Memory, or HBM, the specialized memory towers bolted micrometers away from every AI accelerator.
long_scenes.headline: The AI Memory Supply Crunch
long_scenes.subheadline: Math cores sit idle when memory delivery falls behind
long_scenes.citation_fact: 2025-present global memory shortage driven by AI accelerator HBM demand

long_scenes.narration: Picture a kitchen with ten thousand chefs who can chop ingredients in a microsecond, fed through a single narrow hallway. Standard memory lays chips flat across a circuit board, forcing data down long copper traces. The chefs spend most of their day staring at an empty counter, burning electricity while waiting.
long_scenes.headline: 10,000 Chefs, One Narrow Door
long_scenes.subheadline: Memory bandwidth is bytes per second delivered to the processor
long_scenes.ai_image_prompt: Bright modern daylight tech studio room with large floor-to-ceiling windows and green plants outside, clean flat 2D cel-shaded vector architectural background
long_scenes.citation_fact: Memory bandwidth measures bytes/second delivered across the processor interface

long_scenes.narration: HBM fixes the hallway by building upward. Instead of spreading memory chips across the board, engineers thin each DRAM die until it bends like paper, stack eight or twelve of them vertically, and drill thousands of microscopic vertical elevators called Through-Silicon Vias straight through the silicon.
long_scenes.headline: Vertical Silicon + 1,024 Lanes
long_scenes.subheadline: 3D-stacked DRAM dies linked by Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs)
long_scenes.ai_image_prompt: Clean bright semiconductor design laboratory with sky blue walls and glass partitions, 2D flat cel-shaded vector style, crisp dark ink outlines
long_scenes.citation_fact: 3D-stacked SDRAM connected vertically via Through-Silicon Vias

long_scenes.narration: You still cannot drop a fragile memory tower onto a normal fiberglass board. So chipmakers place the GPU and its HBM stacks side by side on a razor-thin silicon bridge called a 2.5D interposer. Millions of microscopic wires connect them across fractions of a millimeter, slashing energy per bit.
long_scenes.headline: The 2.5D Silicon Interposer
long_scenes.subheadline: Bare dies placed side-by-side on ultra-fine silicon wiring
long_scenes.ai_image_prompt: Cross-section flat cel-shaded 2D vector illustration of a glowing processor die and four vertical memory towers sitting side by side on a sleek silver silicon wafer bridge, clean outlines
long_scenes.citation_fact: 2.5D packaging places HBM stacks and compute dies side-by-side on an interposer

long_scenes.narration: Independent hardware benchmarks show why architects pay the premium. Even an early two-stack HBM subsystem delivered 425 gigabytes per second of real measured bandwidth, beating dual-socket server CPUs by up to 12.9 times on database joins and 3.2 times on machine learning training.
long_scenes.headline: Measured HBM Speedup
long_scenes.subheadline: Hardware benchmarks on data-intensive compute workloads
long_scenes.citation_fact: arXiv Shuhai & FPGA+HBM benchmarks: 425 GB/s measured, up to 12.9x speedup

long_scenes.narration: Yet HBM has a catch: you can only fit a handful of stacks around one GPU package. Research on H100 inference shows that once giant AI models and embedding tables outgrow on-package HBM, engineers must split them across multiple GPUs, paying heavy network synchronization penalties.

long_scenes.narration: Samsung had bigger factories and even unveiled HBM with built-in AI processing in 2021. Apple tapped SK Hynix for custom high-speed DRAM on Vision Pro's R1 chip at 256 gigabytes per second. By perfecting heat-dissipating liquid molding between stacked dies, SK Hynix became Nvidia's primary HBM supplier.
long_scenes.headline: Why SK Hynix Beat Bigger Rivals
long_scenes.subheadline: Yield, thermal bonding, and custom silicon partnerships

long_scenes.narration: Because HBM dies are larger, harder to test, and stacked twelve high, one gigabyte of HBM consumes roughly three times more wafer capacity than standard DDR5 memory. As factories shifted cleanrooms toward AI towers, ordinary server and consumer memory tightened across the entire electronics market.
long_scenes.headline: One Tower Eats Three Wafers
long_scenes.subheadline: Shifting fabs to HBM tightens global standard DRAM supply
long_scenes.ai_image_prompt: Clean 2D flat cel-shaded vector illustration of automated semiconductor cleanroom overhead wafer carriers moving glowing silicon wafers above golden production machines
long_scenes.citation_fact: HBM die size and stacking complexity consume far more fab capacity, fueling shortage

long_scenes.narration: And that is the tradeoff. Commodity memory can be sold to anyone, anytime. HBM is custom-built, bonded to a specific GPU layout, and booked a year in advance. What turned SK Hynix from a cyclical underdog into AI's kingmaker now ties its fortune to whether hyperscalers keep spending.
long_scenes.headline: The Tradeoff: Kingmaker's Lock-In
long_scenes.subheadline: Custom pre-sold towers trade commodity flexibility for AI concentration

sources.title: Wikipedia — High Bandwidth Memory
sources.summary: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is a computer memory interface for 3D-stacked synchronous dynamic random-access memory (SDRAM), initially developed by Samsung, AMD and SK Hynix. It is often used in conjunction with performance-oriented graphics accelerators, network devices, FPGAs and ASICs; some CPUs use HBM as on-package cache or RAM, such as the NEC SX-Aurora TSUBASA and Fujitsu A64FX. The first HBM memory chip was produced by SK Hynix in 2013, and the first devices shipped with HBM were the AMD Fiji GPUs in 2015.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Memory bandwidth
sources.summary: Memory bandwidth is the rate at which data can be read from or stored into a semiconductor memory by a processor. Memory bandwidth is usually expressed in units of bytes/second, though this can vary for systems with natural data sizes that are not a multiple of the commonly used 8-bit bytes.

sources.title: Benchmarking High Bandwidth Memory on FPGAs (Zeke Wang, Hongjing Huang, Jie Zhang)
sources.summary: FPGAs are starting to be enhanced with High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) as a way to reduce the memory bandwidth bottleneck encountered in some applications and to give the FPGA more capacity to deal with application state. However, the performance characteristics of HBM are still not well specified, especially in the context of FPGAs. In this paper, we bridge the gap between nominal specifications and actual performance by benchmarkingHBM on a state-of-the-art FPGA, i.e., a Xilinx Alveo U280 featuring a two-stack HBM subsystem. To this end, we propose Shuhai, a benchmarking tool that allows us to demystify all the underlying details of HBM on an FPGA. FPGA-based benchmarking should also provide a more accurate picture of HBM than doing so on CPUs/GPUs, since CPUs/GPUs are noisier systems due to their complex control logic and cache hierarchy. Since the memory itself is complex, leveraging custom hardware logic to benchmark inside an FPGA provides more details as well as accurate and deterministic measurements. We observe that 1) HBM is able to provide up to 425GB/s memory bandwidth, and 2) how HBM is used has a significant impact on performance, which in turn demonstrates the importance
key_facts: We observe that 1) HBM is able to provide up to 425GB/s memory bandwidth, and 2) how HBM is used has a significant impact on performance, which in turn demonstrates the importance of unveiling the performance characteristics of HBM so as to select the best approach.

sources.title: High Bandwidth Memory on FPGAs: A Data Analytics Perspective (Kaan Kara, Christoph Hagleitner, Dionysios Diamantopoulos)
sources.summary: FPGA-based data processing in datacenters is increasing in popularity due to the demands of modern workloads and the ensuing necessity for specialization in hardware. Driven by this trend, vendors are rapidly adapting reconfigurable devices to suit data and compute intensive workloads. Inclusion of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in FPGA devices is a recent example. HBM promises overcoming the bandwidth bottleneck, faced often by FPGA-based accelerators due to their throughput oriented design. In this paper, we study the usage and benefits of HBM on FPGAs from a data analytics perspective. We consider three workloads that are often performed in analytics oriented databases and implement them on FPGA showing in which cases they benefit from HBM: range selection, hash join, and stochastic gradient descent for linear model training. We integrate our designs into a columnar database (MonetDB) and show the trade-offs arising from the integration related to data movement and partitioning. In certain cases, FPGA+HBM based solutions are able to surpass the highest performance provided by either a 2-socket POWER9 system or a 14-core XeonE5 by up to 1.8x (selection), 12.9x (join), and 3.2x (SGD)
key_facts: In certain cases, FPGA+HBM based solutions are able to surpass the highest performance provided by either a 2-socket POWER9 system or a 14-core XeonE5 by up to 1.8x (selection), 12.9x (join), and 3.2x (SGD).

sources.title: Dissecting Embedding Bag Performance in DLRM Inference (Chandrish Ambati, Jing Ding, Trung Diep)
sources.summary: As the size of DLRMs gets larger, the models must be partitioned across multiple GPUs or nodes of GPUs due to the size limitation of total HBM memory that can be packaged in a GPU. This partitioning adds communication and synchronization overhead of sending and receiving data across GPUs. We use the NCCL and NVSHMEM libraries to measure the performance of an Embedding Bag kernel implemented on H100 GPUs. We compare its performance across diOerent batch sizes, number of tables, table sizes, pooling factors, and embedding dimensions. For a large embedding table that spans multiple GPUs, we project the performance slowdown from distributing an embedding table across multiple GPUs.
